source_text: Nam et orandi perseuerantiam et instantiam mandans parabolam iudicis ponit coacti audire uiduam instantia et perseuerantia interpellationum eius. ergo iudicem deum ostendit orandum, non se, si non ipse est iudex. sed (et) subiunxit facturum deum uindictam electorum suorum. si ergo ipse erit uindex qui et iudex, [si] creatorem ergo meliorem deum probauit, quem electorum suorum clamantium ad eum die et nocte uindicem ostendit. et tamen, cum templum creatoris inducit et duos adorantes diuersa mente describit, Pharisaeum in superbia, publicanum in humilitate, ideoque alterum reprobatum, alterum iustificatum descendisse, utique docendo, qua disciplina sit orandum, eum et hic orandum constituit, a quo relaturi essent iam orandi. disciplinam, siue reprobatricem superbiae siue iustificatricem humilitatis. alterius dei nec templum nec oratores nec iudicium inuenio penes Christum, nisi creatoris: illum iubet adorare in humilitate, ut adleuatorem hurnilium, non in superbia, ut destructorem superborum. quem alium adorandum mihi ostendit? qua disciplina? qua spe? neminem, opinor. nam et quam docuit orationem creatori probauimus conuenire. aliud est, si etiam adorari, qua deus optimus et ultro bonus, non uult. 'Sed quis optimus nisi unus, inquit, deus'? non quasi ex duobus diis unum optimum ostenderit, sed (unum) esse optimum deum solum, qui sic unus sit optimus, qua solus deus. et utique optimus qui pluit super iustos et iniustos et solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos, sustinens et alens et iuuans etiam Marcionitas. Denique interrogatus ab illo quodam: praeceptor optime, quid faciens uitam aeternam possidebo? de praeceptis creatoris an ea sciret, id est faceret, expostulauit, ad contestandum praeceptis creatoris uitam adquiri sempiternam, cumque ille principaliora quaeque adfirmasset obseruasse se ab adolescentia: unum, inquit, tibi deest: omnia, quaecumque habes, uende et da pauperibus. et habebis thesaurum in caelo, et ueni, sequere me. age, Marcion, omnesque iam 'commiserones* et 'coodibiles' eius, haeretici, quid audebitis dicere? resciditne Christus priora praecepta non occidendi non adulterandi non furandi non falsum testandi diligendi patrem et matrem, an et illa seruauit et quod deerat adiecit, — quamquam et hoc praeceptum largitionis in egenos ubique diffusum sit in lege et prophetis — uti gloriosissimus ille obseruator praeceptorum pecuniam multo cariorem habiturus traduceretur? saluum eat igitur et hic euangelio: non ueni dissoluere legem et prophetas, sed potius adimplere. simul et cetera dubitatione liberauit manifestando unius esse et 'dei' nomen et (optimi), et uitam aeternam' et 'thesaurum in caelo', et semetipsum cuius praecepta supplendo et conseruauit et auxit, secundum Micheam quoque hoc loco recognoscendus dicentem: si adnuntiauit tibi homo, quid bonum? aut quid a te dominus exquirit quam facere iudicium diligere misericordiam et paratum esse sequi dominum deum tuum? et <homo' enim Christus adnuntians, quid sit bonum: scientiam legis: praecepta, inquit, scis; 'facere iudicium': uende, inquit, quae habes; 'diligere misericordiam': et da, inquit, egenis; «paratum esse [inquitj ire cum domino': et ueni, inquit, sequere me. Tam distincta fuit a primordio Iudaea gens per tribus et populos et familias et domos, ut nemo facile ignorari de genere potuisset, uel de recentibus Augustianis censibus adhuc tunc fortasse pendentibus. Iesus autem Marcionis, — et (si) natus non dubitaretur qui homo uidebatur - utique, qua non natus, nullam potuerat generis sui in publico habuisse notitiam, sed erat unus aliqui deputandus ex his, qui quo(quo) modo ignoti habebantur. cum igitur praetereuntem illum caecus audisset, cur exclamauit: Iesu, fili Dauid, miserere mei, nisi quia filius Dauid, (id) est ex familia Dauid, non temere deputabatur per matrem et fratres, qui aliquando, ex notitia utique, adnuntiati ei fuerant? (sed antecedentes increpabant caecum, uti taceret'. merito, quoniam quidem uociferabatur, non quia de Dauid filio mentiebatur. aut doce increpantes illos scisse, quod Iesus non esset filius Dauid, ut idcirco silentium caeco indixisse credantur. sed et si doceres. facilius illos ignorasse praesumeres quam dominum falsam in se praedicationem sustinere potuisse. 'sed patiens dominus'. non tamen confirmator erroris. immo etiam detector creatoris ut non prius hanc caecitatem hominis illius enubilasset, ne ultra Iesum filium Dauid existimaret? atquin, ne patientiam eius infamaretis nec ullam rationem dissimulationis illi adfigeretis, [ne filium Dauid negaretis manifestissime confirmauit caeci praedicationem et ipsa remuneratione medicinae et testimonio fidei: fides, inquit, tua te saluum fecit. quid uis caecum credidisse? ab alio deo descendisse Iesum ad detectionem creatoris, ad destructionem legis et prophetarum? non illum esse, qui ex radice Iesse et ex fructu lumborum Dauid destinabatur, caecorum quoque remunerator? sed nondum, puto, eiusmodi tunc caeci erant qualis Marcion, ut haec fuerit caeci illius fides, qua crediderit in uoce: Iesu, fili Dauid. qui hoc se et cognouit et cognosci ab omnibus uoluit I fidem hominis, etsi melius oculatam, etsi ueri luminis compotem, exteriore quoque uisione donauit, ut et nos regulam simulque mercedem fidei disceremus: qui uult uidere. Iesum Dauid filium credat per uirginis censum; qui non ita credet, non audiet ab illo: fides tua te saluum fecit, atque ita caecus remanebit, ruens in antithesin, ruentem et ipsam (in) antithesin. sic enim caecus caecum deducere solet. nam si, (quia) aliquando Dauid in recuperatione Sionis offenderant caeci, resistentes quominus admitteretur, — in figuram populi proinde caeci, non admissuri quandoque Christum filium Dauid — ideo Christus ex diuerso caeco subuenit, ut hinc se ostenderet non esse filium Dauid, ut ex animi diuersitate bonus caecis, quos ille iusserat caedi, id cur fidei et quidem prauae praestitisse se dixit? atquin et hoc (filius Dauid' (dat) antithesin de suo retundendam. nam quia Dauid offenderant caeci, nunc uero eiusdem t carnis homo supplicem se obtulerat filio Dauid, idcirco ei satisfacienti quodammodo placatus filius Dauid restituit lumina cum testimonio fidei, qua hoc ipsum crediderat exorandum sibi esse filium Dauid. et tamen Dauid audacia hominum, puto, offenderat, non ualitudo.
pass_a_gloss: For He commands perseverance and insistence in prayer, setting forth a parable of a judge, forced to hear a widow by her insistence and perseverance in her petitions. Therefore, He shows that God is to be prayed to, not Himself, if He is not the judge. But He also added that God will execute vengeance for His elect. If, therefore, He will be the avenger who is also the judge, then He has proved the Creator to be the better God, whom He shows to be the avenger of His elect, who cry out to Him day and night. And yet, when He introduces the temple of the Creator and describes two people worshiping with different minds, a Pharisee in pride and a publican in humility, and therefore one is rejected and the other justified, He is teaching by what discipline one ought to pray, and He establishes that one ought to pray to Him from whom they will receive the discipline of prayer, whether it reproves pride or justifies humility. I do not find the temple or worshipers or judgment of another God with Christ, except that of the Creator: He commands to worship in humility, as the helper of the humble, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. Who else does He show me to worship? By what discipline? By what hope? No one, I think. For even the prayer that He taught, we have proved to be suitable for the Creator. It is different if He also does not want to be worshiped, as the best and kindest God. 'But who is the best, except the one God?' He does not show one of two gods to be the best, but that the one God is the best, who is the only good God, because He is the only God. And certainly, He is the best who rains on the just and the unjust and makes His sun rise over the good and the evil, sustaining and nourishing and helping even the Marcionites. Finally, when someone asked Him, 'Good Teacher, what shall I do to possess eternal life?' He inquired whether he knew the commandments of the Creator, that is, whether he did them, to testify that eternal life is acquired by the commandments of the Creator. And when he had affirmed that he had observed the principal commandments from his youth, He said, 'One thing you lack: sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me.' Come, Marcion, and all your fellow-feelers and co-worshipers, heretics, what will you dare to say? Did Christ abolish the former commandments, 'Do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother,' or did He also keep those and add what was lacking? Although this commandment of giving to the poor is also diffused everywhere in the law and the prophets, so that the most glorious observer of the commandments, having much more precious money, would be led astray? Let him go, therefore, and this Gospel: 'I did not come to destroy the law and the prophets, but to fulfill.' At the same time, He freed the other doubts, manifesting that the name of God and the best, and eternal life and treasure in heaven, belong to one, and that He Himself, whose commandments He was supplementing and conserving and increasing, is recognized according to Micah, who says in this place: 'If a man has announced to you what is good, or what does the Lord require of you, except to do justice, to love mercy, and to be prepared to follow the Lord your God?' And Christ, announcing what is good, says, 'You know the commandments; do justice,' He says, 'sell what you have; love mercy,' He says, 'and give to the poor; be prepared to follow the Lord,' He says, 'and come, follow me.' The Jewish people were so distinct from the beginning, divided into tribes and peoples and families and houses, that no one could easily be ignorant of their kind or family, even from the recent Augustan censuses, which were perhaps still pending at that time. But Jesus, according to Marcion, - and if He was not born, it would not be doubted who He seemed to be - certainly, because He was not born, He could not have had any public knowledge of His kind, but He would have been considered one of those who were unknown in some way. When, therefore, a blind man heard Him passing by, why did he cry out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me,' unless He was not rashly considered the Son of David, that is, from the family of David, through His mother and brothers, who had sometime been announced to him, from knowledge, of course? But those who came before rebuked the blind man, that he should be silent, rightly, because he was crying out, not because he was lying about being the Son of David. Or does He teach that those who rebuked him knew that Jesus was not the Son of David, so that they are believed to have imposed silence on the blind man for that reason? But even if He taught, it would be easier to presume that they were ignorant than that the Lord could have endured a false proclamation about Himself. 'But the Lord is patient,' not, however, a confirmer of error. On the contrary, He is also the detector of the Creator, so that He did not previously dispel the blindness of that man, lest he think Jesus to be the Son of David. But, lest you defame His patience or attach any reason for dissimulation to Him, He clearly confirmed the blind man's proclamation, both by the reward of healing and by the testimony of faith: 'Your faith has saved you.' What do you want the blind man to have believed? That Jesus came down from another God to detect the Creator, to destroy the law and the prophets? Is He not the one who was destined from the root of Jesse and from the fruit of the loins of David, the rewarder of the blind? But, I think, the blind men were not yet of such a kind as Marcion, so that this was the faith of that blind man, that he believed in the voice, 'Jesus, Son of David,' who knew Himself and wanted to be known by all, and He gave the faith of the man, even if it was better to be sighted, even if it was endowed with the true light, also an external vision, so that we might learn the rule and reward of faith at the same time: whoever wants to see, let him believe Jesus to be the Son of David through the census of the Virgin; whoever does not believe thus, will not hear from Him, 'Your faith has saved you,' and thus the blind man will remain, rushing into contradiction, and rushing into contradiction himself. For the blind man usually leads the blind. For if, because the blind men had sometime offended David in the recovery of Zion, resisting so that he might not be admitted, - in figure, therefore, of a blind people, not admitting Christ the Son of David - therefore Christ helps the blind man in a different way, so that He might show Himself not to be the Son of David, as if, from a diversity of mind, He is good to the blind, whom He had ordered to be killed, why did He say that He had endured false faith? But, on the contrary, this 'Son of David' gives a contradiction to be blunted. For because the blind men had offended David, now, however, a man of the same flesh offered himself as a suppliant to the Son of David, and therefore, satisfying him in some way, the Son of David, placated, restored his sight, with the testimony of faith, by which he had believed that this very thing was to be prayed for, that he might be the Son of David. And yet, I think, David had offended the audacity of men, not their strength.

pass_b_english: Jesus commands perseverance and insistence in prayer, putting forward the parable of a judge forced to hear a widow because of her insistence and perseverance in petitioning him. He therefore shows that God is the one to be prayed to, not himself — unless he himself is the judge. But he also adds that God will execute vengeance for his elect. If, then, he is to be the avenger who is also the judge, he has thereby proved the Creator to be the better God, the one he shows as the avenger of his elect who cry out to him day and night. And yet, when he brings in the Creator's temple and describes two worshipers with different dispositions — a Pharisee in pride, a tax collector in humility — with the result that one is rejected and the other justified, he is teaching by what discipline one ought to pray. He establishes that one must pray to the very God from whom they will receive that discipline of prayer, whether it condemns pride or justifies humility. I find no temple, no worshipers, and no judgment belonging to any other God in Christ except the Creator's. He commands worship in humility, as the helper of the humble, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. Who else does he show me to worship? By what discipline? By what hope? No one, I think. For even the prayer he taught, we have proved, suits the Creator. It would be a different matter if he also refuses to be worshiped, since he is the best and kindest God. 'But who is best except the one God?' He does not present one of two gods as the best, but that the one God alone is best — best because he alone is God. And he is certainly the best who rains on the just and the unjust and makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, sustaining and nourishing and helping even Marcionites (Matthew 5:45).

Finally, when someone asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' he challenged him on whether he knew the Creator's commandments — that is, whether he kept them — to testify that eternal life is acquired by the Creator's commandments. When the man affirmed he had kept the principal ones from his youth, Jesus said, 'One thing you lack: sell everything you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.' Come now, Marcion, and all you fellow-feelers and co-worshipers, heretics — what will you dare say? Did Christ abolish the former commandments — do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother — or did he keep those and add what was lacking? Although this command to give to the poor is spread throughout the Law and the Prophets, so that the most glorious keeper of the commandments, who valued his money far more, would be led astray? Let this Gospel stand: 'I did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them.' At the same time he resolved the other doubts, making clear that the name of God, and the Best, and eternal life, and treasure in heaven belong to one God, and that he himself — whose commandments he was supplementing, conserving, and increasing — is recognized in Micah, who says in this place: 'He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God?' (Micah 6:8). And Christ, announcing what is good: 'You know the commandments' — that is the knowledge of the Law; 'Do justice,' he says, 'sell what you have'; 'Love mercy,' he says, 'and give to the poor'; 'Be prepared to follow the Lord,' he says, 'and come, follow me.'

The Jewish people were so distinct from the beginning, divided into tribes, peoples, families, and houses, that no one could easily be ignorant of their lineage — even from the recent Augustan censuses, which were perhaps still underway at that time. But Jesus, according to Marcion — and if he was not born, it would not be doubted that he seemed a man — certainly, because he was not born, he could have had no public knowledge of his lineage; he would simply have been counted among those unknown in some way. So when a blind man heard him passing by, why did he cry out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me,' unless he was not rashly considered the Son of David — that is, from the family of David — through his mother and brothers, who had at some point been made known to him, presumably from public knowledge? Those going before rebuked the blind man to silence — rightly, because he was shouting, not because he was lying about the Son of David. Or are you teaching that the rebukers knew Jesus was not the Son of David, so that they supposedly imposed silence on the blind man for that reason? But even if you taught that, it would be easier to presume they were ignorant than that the Lord could have endured a false proclamation about himself. 'But the Lord is patient' — yet not a confirmer of error. On the contrary, he is also the detector of the Creator, as if he did not previously dispel that man's blindness lest he think Jesus was the Son of David. But lest you defame his patience or pin any motive of dissimulation on him, he plainly confirmed the blind man's proclamation both by the reward of healing and by the testimony of faith: 'Your faith has saved you.' What do you want the blind man to have believed? That Jesus descended from another God to detect the Creator, to destroy the Law and the Prophets? Is he not the one destined from the root of Jesse and the fruit of David's loins, the rewarder even of the blind? But I think the blind were not yet of Marcion's stripe, so that this was the faith of that blind man — that he believed in the cry, 'Jesus, Son of David.'

The one who knew himself and wanted to be known by all gave the man's faith — even if better sighted, even if endowed with true light — also an external vision, so that we might learn both the rule and the reward of faith at once: whoever wants to see, let him believe Jesus to be the Son of David through the census of the Virgin; whoever does not believe thus will not hear from him, 'Your faith has saved you,' and so will remain blind, rushing into contradiction, and dragging the contradiction itself down with him. For the blind typically lead the blind. For if the blind once offended David during the recovery of Zion, resisting his admission — a figure, therefore, of a blind people who would not admit Christ the Son of David — then Christ helps a blind man in the opposite way, to show himself not to be the Son of David? As if, from a diversity of mind, he is good to the blind whom David ordered killed — why then did he say he endured false faith? On the contrary, this 'Son of David' returns a contradiction to be blunted. Because the blind offended David, but now a man of the very same flesh offered himself as a suppliant to the Son of David, the Son of David, placated by satisfying him in a way, restored his sight with the testimony of faith by which he had believed this very thing was to be prayed for — that he might be the Son of David. And yet, I think, David was offended by the audacity of men, not by their infirmity.
notes: The text is a commentary on the Gospel of Luke, specifically the parable of the persistent widow (Luke 18:1-8) and the story of the blind man (Luke 18:35-43).

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the complex theological arguments regarding the Creator vs. the Marcionite God, the identity of the Son of David, and the interpretation of the blind man's healing. Scripture citations (Matthew 5:45 and Micah 6:8) are correctly added to the English text to match the Latin allusions. All clauses in the Latin are accounted for in Pass A and B.

source: 'Nam et orandi perseuerantiam et instantiam mandans parabolam iudicis ponit coacti audire uiduam instantia et perseuerantia interpellationum eius.', english: 'For He commands perseverance and insistence in prayer, setting forth a parable of a judge, forced to hear a widow by her insistence and perseverance in her petitions.'
